pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l01.q: A stimulus is made twice as intense. How does a single neuron encode that increase?
choices: By firing more frequently, since each spike is all-or-none
By lowering its resting potential to -140 mV
By releasing a different neurotransmitter
By producing an action potential twice as large
pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l01.why: Action potentials are all-or-none, so intensity is coded by firing frequency and by how many neurons are recruited, not by spike amplitude. Resting potential stays near -70 mV and the transmitter a neuron releases does not change with intensity.

pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l01.q: Which cell lays down myelin in the peripheral nerves, and which does it in the brain and spinal cord?
choices: Astrocytes in both
Microglia peripherally, astrocytes centrally
Schwann cells peripherally, oligodendrocytes centrally
Oligodendrocytes peripherally, Schwann cells centrally
pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l01.why: Schwann cells myelinate peripheral axons and oligodendrocytes myelinate central ones, which is why Guillain-Barre is peripheral and multiple sclerosis is central. Astrocytes support the blood-brain barrier and microglia are immune cells; neither makes myelin.

pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l02.q: A patient with a right parietal stroke shaves only the right half of his face and denies that his left arm belongs to him. What is this called and why does it follow a right-sided lesion?
choices: Expressive aphasia, because Broca's area is on the right in most people
Hemineglect, because spatial attention lives in the non-dominant parietal lobe
Dementia, because self-recognition is a memory function
Cerebellar ataxia, because the parietal lobe coordinates movement
pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l02.why: Non-dominant parietal damage produces neglect of the contralateral world, including the patient's own limb. Language and Broca's area sit in the dominant hemisphere, which is left in about 95 percent of right-handers, and coordination is cerebellar.

pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l02.q: Which structure provides arousal, so that damage to it leaves a patient unable to wake even with an intact cortex?
choices: The occipital cortex
The hippocampus
The basal ganglia
The reticular activating system in the brainstem and thalamus
pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l02.why: Arousal comes from the reticular activating system while content comes from the cortex, so RAS damage produces coma despite intact cortical tissue. The hippocampus forms memory, the basal ganglia smooth movement, and the occipital cortex handles vision.

pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l03.q: A patient has an ICP of 30 mmHg. What MAP is required to keep cerebral perfusion pressure at the target of at least 60 mmHg?
choices: At least 30 mmHg
MAP does not affect CPP
At least 90 mmHg
At least 60 mmHg
pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l03.why: CPP = MAP - ICP, so 60 + 30 requires a MAP of at least 90 mmHg. Allowing the MAP to sit at 60 with an ICP of 30 leaves a CPP of only 30, which is why hypotension is as dangerous as intracranial hypertension.

pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l03.q: A CT shows a convex lens-shaped collection over the right temporal region that stops abruptly at the coronal suture. Which bleed is this and why does it stop there?
choices: Epidural hematoma, because the dura is anchored at suture lines
Intraparenchymal hemorrhage confined by white matter tracts
Subdural hematoma, because veins stop at sutures
Subarachnoid hemorrhage, which follows the sulci
pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l03.why: Epidural blood strips the dura off the skull but cannot pass where the dura is firmly anchored at sutures, giving a lens shape that respects them. Subdural blood is crescentic and crosses sutures, and subarachnoid blood fills the cisterns and sulci.

pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l04.q: Why does an MCA stroke weaken the face and arm more than the leg?
choices: The MCA supplies only sensory cortex
Leg muscles are stronger and resist ischemia
The leg has bilateral innervation
The motor homunculus places face and hand on the lateral surface, MCA territory, while the leg sits over the top edge in ACA territory
pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l04.why: The homunculus puts face and hand on the lateral convexity fed by the MCA and tucks the leg area onto the medial surface fed by the ACA. Leg muscle strength and bilateral innervation are not the explanation, and the MCA supplies both motor and sensory cortex.

pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l04.q: A patient with a large vessel occlusion presents 11 hours after last known well. Is any reperfusion therapy possible?
choices: No, all reperfusion windows close at 4.5 hours
Yes, mechanical thrombectomy can be offered out to 24 hours in selected patients whose imaging shows salvageable penumbra
Yes, thrombolytics are given up to 24 hours
Only if the patient has a TIA rather than a stroke
pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l04.why: Thrombolysis is generally limited to 4.5 hours, but thrombectomy extends to 24 hours in selected large vessel occlusions when imaging still shows penumbra worth saving. A TIA by definition has no infarct and is not the target of thrombectomy.

pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l05.q: Light shone in the right eye produces no constriction in either pupil, but light in the left eye constricts both. Where is the lesion?
choices: Left oculomotor nerve
Right optic nerve, an afferent defect
Right oculomotor nerve, an efferent defect
Left optic nerve
pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l05.why: The right pupil constricts consensually when the left eye is lit, proving the efferent CN III pathway works; the failure occurs only when light enters the right eye, localizing to the right optic nerve. A CN III lesion would leave the pupil fixed regardless of which eye is lit.

pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l05.q: A patient's tongue deviates to the right when protruded. Which nerve is affected and on which side?
choices: Right facial nerve
Left vagus nerve
Left hypoglossal nerve
Right hypoglossal nerve
pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l05.why: The tongue deviates toward the weak side, so rightward deviation means a right hypoglossal (CN XII) lesion. The facial nerve moves the face rather than the tongue body, and the vagus affects palate and voice.

pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l06.q: A patient has brisk 3+ reflexes at both knees with upgoing toes and no muscle wasting. What does this localize?
choices: An upper motor neuron problem in the brain or spinal cord
A neuromuscular junction problem
A primary muscle disease
A lower motor neuron problem at the nerve root
pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l06.why: Hyperreflexia with a positive Babinski and preserved bulk is the upper motor neuron pattern, meaning brain or cord. Lower motor neuron lesions give absent reflexes with flaccid wasting muscle, and junction and muscle diseases do not produce an upgoing toe.

pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l06.q: A trauma patient has no movement or sensation below T6 but does report faint perianal sensation. Why does this finding change the prognosis?
choices: It has no prognostic value
It proves the injury is at a lower level than T6
Sacral sparing makes the injury incomplete, which carries a far better prognosis than a complete injury
It confirms spinal shock rather than injury
pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l06.why: Any preserved function below the level, including perianal sensation or voluntary anal squeeze, defines an incomplete injury and predicts better recovery. Sacral sparing does not relocate the level and is not the same as spinal shock.

pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l07.q: Why does clonidine lower blood pressure even though it is a receptor agonist rather than a blocker?
choices: It stimulates beta-2 receptors on arterioles
It blocks muscarinic receptors in the heart
It stimulates alpha-1 receptors on veins
It stimulates alpha-2 receptors, which reduce norepinephrine release and lower central sympathetic outflow
pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l07.why: Alpha-2 receptors are presynaptic and central autoreceptors, so stimulating them turns sympathetic output down. Alpha-1 stimulation would raise pressure, muscarinic blockade raises heart rate, and clonidine is not a beta-2 agonist.

pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l07.q: A patient poisoned with an organophosphate has been given 2 mg of atropine and the heart rate has risen from 44 to 96, but the patient is still drowning in bronchial secretions. What should happen next?
choices: Stop atropine, since the heart rate target has been reached
Continue escalating atropine until the secretions dry, because secretions are the endpoint and what kills
Switch to naloxone
Give a beta blocker to bring the rate back down
pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l07.why: Atropine in cholinergic poisoning is titrated to drying pulmonary secretions, not to a heart rate, because bronchorrhea is the lethal feature. Naloxone treats opioids, and blunting the rate would leave the secretions untreated.

pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l08.q: A patient opens his eyes only to painful pressure, says nothing at all, and localizes to the stimulus by reaching above the clavicle. What is the GCS?
choices: GCS 6 (E2 V2 M2)
GCS 7 (E2 V1 M4)
GCS 8 (E2 V1 M5)
GCS 9 (E3 V1 M5)
pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l08.why: Eye opening to pressure is 2, no verbal response is 1, and localizing by crossing midline or reaching above the clavicle is motor 5, totalling 8. Withdrawal without aiming would be motor 4, giving 7.

pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l08.q: Why does a benzodiazepine become less effective the longer a seizure has run?
choices: GABA receptors internalize after roughly 30 minutes of continuous seizure activity
Glutamate receptors are destroyed early in the seizure
Benzodiazepines only work on focal seizures
The drug is metabolized faster during seizures
pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l08.why: Prolonged status causes GABA-A receptors to be pulled off the membrane, so the drug has fewer targets, which is the argument for treating early at full dose. Metabolic rate and glutamate receptor destruction are not the mechanism.

pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l09.q: A 34-year-old has a compartment pressure of 38 mmHg in the anterior leg with a diastolic blood pressure of 62 mmHg. What is the delta pressure and what does it indicate?
choices: Delta 24 mmHg, under the threshold of 30, supporting fasciotomy
Delta 38 mmHg, reassuring
Delta 100 mmHg, normal
Delta cannot be calculated without an arterial line
pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l09.why: Delta pressure is diastolic minus compartment pressure, 62 - 38 = 24 mmHg, and a value under 30 supports fasciotomy, as does an absolute pressure above about 30 mmHg. The delta is a subtraction, not a sum, and a cuff diastolic is sufficient.

pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l09.q: A 7-year-old has a fracture line running straight across the growth plate only, with no metaphyseal or epiphyseal extension. Which Salter-Harris type is this?
choices: Type III
Type V
Type I
Type II
pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l09.why: SALTR: type I is Straight across the physis alone, type II extends Above into the metaphysis and is the most common, type III goes beLow into the epiphysis, and type V is a cRush injury that may look aligned on film.

pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l10.q: A patient with an inversion ankle injury can take four steps in the department and has no tenderness over either malleolus, the navicular, or the fifth metatarsal base. What do the Ottawa rules advise?
choices: X-ray the foot only
No imaging is required
CT the ankle
X-ray both the ankle and the foot
pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l10.why: The Ottawa rules require imaging only for bone tenderness at the malleolar tips or posterior edges, the navicular, or the fifth metatarsal base, or an inability to take four steps; none applies here. The rules are close to 100 percent sensitive for significant fractures when applied correctly.

pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l10.q: A 52-year-old felt a sudden blow to the back of the ankle while pushing off during tennis. Squeezing the calf produces no plantar flexion. What does this test show?
choices: A positive McMurray test indicating a meniscal tear
A positive drawer test indicating an ankle sprain
A positive Lachman test indicating an ACL tear
A positive Thompson test indicating an Achilles tendon rupture
pa-anatomy-neuro-msk-l10.why: The Thompson test squeezes the calf to check tendon continuity, and absent plantar flexion means the Achilles is ruptured. Lachman and McMurray are knee tests, and an ankle sprain leaves the calf squeeze intact.

quiz.q: A neuron's membrane is depolarized from -70 mV to -60 mV by an incoming signal, but no action potential occurs. What best explains this?
choices: Threshold near -55 mV was not reached, and the response is all-or-none
The axon is unmyelinated
The neuron is in its absolute refractory period by definition
The sodium-potassium ATPase has failed
quiz.why: Voltage-gated sodium channels open only once the membrane reaches roughly -55 mV, and below that nothing fires because the response is all-or-none. Pump failure would abolish the resting gradient entirely, myelination changes speed rather than threshold, and refractoriness cannot be assumed.

quiz.q: Why does the refractory period matter functionally?
choices: It lets sodium enter continuously
It allows the action potential to grow larger along the axon
It prevents the impulse from traveling backward, forcing one-way conduction
It permits tetanic summation in nerve
quiz.why: During refractoriness the segment just depolarized cannot fire again, so the impulse can only move forward. Action potentials do not grow in size, and the refractory period limits rather than permits summation.

quiz.q: A patient with multiple sclerosis has slowed conduction in the optic nerve. Which structure is damaged and what is the physiologic consequence?
choices: The sodium-potassium ATPase, so the resting potential collapses
The myelin sheath, so saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier is lost and velocity falls
The axon hillock, so action potentials cannot be generated
The synaptic vesicles, so no transmitter is released
quiz.why: Demyelination exposes membrane between nodes and eliminates the jumping conduction that gives large fibers speeds up to about 120 m/s. The axon itself, the vesicles and the pump are not the primary targets in demyelinating disease.

quiz.q: Haloperidol produces rigidity and a shuffling gait in a young patient. Which transmitter system explains this adverse effect?
choices: Blocked NMDA glutamate receptors
Increased serotonin reuptake
Enhanced GABA transmission
Blocked dopamine receptors, producing a drug-induced parkinsonism
quiz.why: Antipsychotics block dopamine, reproducing the movement disorder seen when nigral dopamine neurons die in Parkinson's disease. GABA enhancement sedates, NMDA blockade is the mechanism of ketamine, and serotonin changes do not cause this picture.

quiz.q: A 63-year-old cannot produce fluent speech but follows multi-step commands accurately and is visibly frustrated by his own errors. Where is the lesion?
choices: The occipital cortex
Wernicke's area in the dominant temporal lobe
Broca's area in the dominant frontal lobe
The non-dominant parietal lobe
quiz.why: Preserved comprehension with impaired output and awareness of the deficit is an expressive Broca's aphasia in the dominant frontal lobe. A Wernicke's aphasia is fluent nonsense with poor comprehension and little insight, and parietal or occipital lesions do not primarily impair speech output.

quiz.q: A patient has a right-sided intention tremor that worsens as the finger approaches the target, right-sided dysmetria, and a wide-based gait. Where is the lesion?
choices: Right cerebellar hemisphere, because cerebellar findings are ipsilateral
Left cerebellar hemisphere
Right basal ganglia
Left cerebral cortex, because motor findings are contralateral
quiz.why: Cerebellar signs appear on the same side as the lesion, unlike cortical motor and sensory findings, which cross. Basal ganglia disease produces resting tremor and rigidity rather than intention tremor and dysmetria.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old with no psychiatric history develops disorganized thinking and hallucinations over 12 hours with fluctuating attention. What framing is most appropriate?
choices: Early dementia
Malingering
New-onset primary psychosis, which commonly begins at this age with fluctuating attention
Delirium from a medical cause, because attention is impaired and the course fluctuates acutely
quiz.why: Impaired attention with an acute fluctuating course defines delirium and demands a search for infection, drugs, glucose or sodium abnormalities. Primary psychosis leaves attention and orientation intact, and dementia progresses over months to years.

quiz.q: Which subcortical structure relays nearly every sensory modality to the cortex, with the exception of smell?
choices: Hypothalamus
Thalamus
Cerebellum
Basal ganglia
quiz.why: The thalamus is the sensory relay station, and olfaction is the one modality that bypasses it. The hypothalamus governs temperature, hunger and the pituitary, the cerebellum coordinates movement, and the basal ganglia smooth it.

quiz.q: A patient with a severe headache has a normal non-contrast head CT performed 14 hours after symptom onset. What is the next step if subarachnoid hemorrhage is still suspected?
choices: Discharge, since CT excludes the diagnosis at any time point
Lumbar puncture looking for xanthochromia
Repeat the same CT in 24 hours
Start empiric antibiotics for meningitis
quiz.why: CT sensitivity for subarachnoid blood is very high within 6 hours and falls afterward, so a lumbar puncture for xanthochromia is used beyond that window. Repeating an identical CT adds little, and antibiotics do not address the suspected diagnosis.

quiz.q: A head-injured patient develops a fixed, dilated right pupil with left-sided weakness. What is happening anatomically?
choices: Tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum
A left middle cerebral artery stroke
Bilateral optic nerve injury
Uncal herniation compressing the right cranial nerve III, with the motor tract crossing below to produce left-sided weakness
quiz.why: The medial temporal lobe presses over the tentorium onto the ipsilateral CN III, giving a blown pupil on the side of the lesion, while the corticospinal tract crosses in the medulla so weakness appears on the opposite side. Tonsillar herniation compresses the medulla and stops breathing rather than blowing one pupil.

quiz.q: Why does compensation for a slowly expanding intracranial mass end abruptly rather than gradually?
choices: Once displaceable CSF and venous blood have been expelled, the fixed skull leaves nothing left to give, so small further volume causes steep pressure rises
Cerebral arteries dilate to make room
The skull expands slightly in adults
Brain tissue can be compressed indefinitely
quiz.why: The Monro-Kellie doctrine describes a fixed box holding brain, blood and CSF, and only CSF and venous blood can be displaced; once they are gone, the pressure-volume curve turns nearly vertical. The adult skull does not expand and arterial dilation would raise volume further.

quiz.q: Brief hyperventilation to an EtCO2 of 30 to 35 mmHg lowers intracranial pressure by which mechanism, and why is it not used routinely?
choices: It reduces brain metabolic rate, but causes seizures
It increases CSF absorption, but causes hydrocephalus
It constricts cerebral vessels, reducing intracranial blood volume, but that same constriction reduces cerebral blood flow
It dilates cerebral vessels, but raises blood pressure
quiz.why: Lowering PaCO2 constricts cerebral arterioles and shrinks blood volume within minutes, but that comes at the cost of perfusion, so it is a bridge for active herniation rather than a routine therapy. It does not change CSF absorption or dilate vessels.

quiz.q: A patient has a dense left homonymous hemianopia with completely normal strength, sensation and speech. Which vessel is most likely occluded?
choices: Left anterior cerebral artery
Basilar artery
Right middle cerebral artery
Right posterior cerebral artery
quiz.why: Isolated visual field loss with intact strength points to the occipital cortex, supplied by the posterior cerebral artery on the side opposite the field cut. An MCA stroke would add face and arm weakness, and an ACA stroke would weaken the leg.

quiz.q: A 70-year-old has vertigo, double vision, slurred speech and cannot sit unsupported. What is the concern and why is it easily missed?
choices: Peripheral vertigo, missed because it is benign
Posterior circulation stroke, missed because dizziness and nausea mimic a vestibular problem
Anterior cerebral artery stroke, missed because leg weakness is subtle
Migraine with aura, missed because of the age
quiz.why: Dizziness in company with diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia or truncal instability is a vertebrobasilar stroke until proven otherwise. Isolated benign vertigo does not produce double vision or an inability to sit, and ACA strokes do not cause these findings.

quiz.q: Which statement about the Circle of Willis is correct?
choices: It has no relationship to aneurysm formation
It is anatomically complete in nearly everyone, so occlusions rarely cause deficits
It is complete in only about 20 to 50 percent of people, which partly explains why identical occlusions cause different deficits
It connects only the two vertebral arteries
quiz.why: The ring is a collateral pathway present in complete form in a minority of people, so collateral rescue varies widely between patients. It joins anterior and posterior circulations, and it is the commonest site of berry aneurysms, especially at the anterior communicating artery.

quiz.q: A patient with stroke symptoms has a fingerstick glucose of 34 mg/dL. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: Hypoglycemia can imitate a focal stroke exactly and must be corrected immediately before attributing the deficit to ischemia
Glucose has no relationship to focal deficits
Thrombolysis should proceed regardless
The glucose result indicates a posterior circulation stroke
quiz.why: Hypoglycemia is a classic stroke mimic and is reversible in seconds, which is why glucose is checked on every suspected stroke. Proceeding to thrombolysis without correcting it risks treating a non-ischemic, fixable problem.

quiz.q: Why does a cortical stroke spare the forehead while Bell's palsy does not?
choices: The forehead receives input from both hemispheres, so one cortical lesion leaves it working, while the peripheral nerve carries the whole half of the face
Bell's palsy affects only the lower face
The forehead is supplied by the trigeminal nerve
The forehead has no motor innervation
quiz.why: Bilateral cortical input to the forehead protects it in a central lesion, but the facial nerve itself serves the entire ipsilateral face, so a peripheral palsy takes the forehead too. The trigeminal nerve carries facial sensation, not forehead movement.

quiz.q: A patient has ptosis with a dilated pupil and an eye resting down and out. Which cranial nerve is involved and what must be excluded urgently in a head-injured patient?
choices: Cranial nerve IV; a trochlear palsy
Cranial nerve VI; raised intracranial pressure
Cranial nerve III; uncal herniation
Cranial nerve VII; Bell's palsy
quiz.why: The oculomotor nerve carries eyelid elevation, pupillary constriction and most eye movement, so its loss gives ptosis, a blown pupil and a down-and-out eye, which in head injury means herniation until proven otherwise. CN VI produces isolated failure of abduction and CN IV vertical diplopia.

quiz.q: Which bedside test is the most informative single element of the neurologic exam and also the one most often skipped?
choices: Pupillary size measurement
Gait, because walking requires motor, sensory, cerebellar and vestibular systems working together
Deep tendon reflexes
Two-point discrimination
quiz.why: Gait integrates several systems at once, so an abnormality flags disease even when isolated tests look normal. Reflexes, discrimination and pupil size each probe only a narrow part of the nervous system.

quiz.q: A patient after a stroke has a unilaterally absent gag and a palate that fails to rise on the left. Which nerves are involved and what practical risk follows?
choices: CN XI and XII, with risk of shoulder droop
CN III and IV, with risk of diplopia
CN V and VII, with risk of corneal injury
CN IX and X, with risk of aspiration
quiz.why: Glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves mediate the gag and palatal elevation, and their loss makes swallowing unsafe. The other pairs govern facial sensation and movement, shoulder and tongue, and eye movement respectively.

quiz.q: A patient has a hemisection of the cord on the left at T8. Which combination is expected below the injury?
choices: Bilateral weakness with preserved sensation
Left loss of pain and temperature only
Left weakness and left loss of vibration, with right loss of pain and temperature
Right weakness and right loss of vibration, with left loss of pain and temperature
quiz.why: Corticospinal and dorsal column fibers have already crossed or cross later in the medulla, so their loss is ipsilateral, while spinothalamic fibers cross within one or two levels of entry, so pain and temperature loss appears contralaterally. That combination is Brown-Sequard syndrome.

quiz.q: A patient has intact sensation at the nipple line and absent sensation below it. Which sensory level is this?
choices: T4
L1
C4
quiz.why: The nipple line is the T4 dermatome anchor, while C4 covers the top of the shoulders, T10 the umbilicus and L1 the groin. Getting the anchors right is what allows a level to be assigned at the bedside.

quiz.q: A patient with a fresh C6 injury has flaccid paralysis with absent reflexes but a blood pressure of 128/76 and a heart rate of 84. What is the correct term for this state?
choices: Hypovolemic shock
Cauda equina syndrome
Neurogenic shock
Spinal shock
quiz.why: Spinal shock is the temporary neurologic shutdown of the cord below the injury, giving flaccid areflexia with no blood pressure abnormality; its resolution is signalled by the return of the bulbocavernosus reflex. Neurogenic shock is a circulatory state with hypotension and bradycardia, which is absent here.

quiz.q: Which root level is tested by the Achilles reflex, and which movement does that root control?
choices: C7, elbow extension
S1, ankle plantar flexion
L5, big toe extension
L4, knee extension
quiz.why: The Achilles reflex tests S1, the same root that drives plantar flexion, which is why an S1 radiculopathy weakens push-off and dampens the reflex. The patellar reflex tests L4 and the triceps reflex C7, and L5 has no reliable deep tendon reflex.

quiz.q: A 45-year-old with a large central disc herniation at L4 to L5 cannot void, has numbness over the buttocks and inner thighs, and has reduced anal tone. What is the correct action?
choices: Conservative management with physical therapy and reassessment in two weeks
Urgent MRI and surgical consultation, because this is cauda equina syndrome
Outpatient nerve conduction studies
Bed rest with opioids and a follow-up appointment
quiz.why: Saddle anesthesia, urinary retention and lost anal tone define cauda equina syndrome, a surgical emergency in which delay costs permanent bladder and sexual function. Conservative management, nerve studies and bed rest all waste the window.

quiz.q: Which statement about autonomic anatomy is correct?
choices: Sympathetic fibers leave from S2 to S4 and act locally
Parasympathetic ganglia lie next to the spinal cord
Acetylcholine is the transmitter at all sympathetic effector organs
Sympathetic fibers leave from T1 to L2 and synapse in a paravertebral chain, producing a broad response
quiz.why: Sympathetic outflow is thoracolumbar with ganglia near the cord and wide divergence, producing a whole-body broadcast, while parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral with ganglia on the target organ. Norepinephrine is the usual sympathetic effector transmitter, with sweat glands as the cholinergic exception.

quiz.q: A patient takes tamsulosin for benign prostatic hyperplasia and faints when standing. Which receptor action explains the hypotension?
choices: Alpha-1 blockade preventing vasoconstriction on standing
Muscarinic blockade causing tachycardia
Beta-2 stimulation causing bronchodilation
Beta-1 blockade reducing contractility
quiz.why: Alpha-1 receptors constrict arterioles and veins, so blocking them removes the reflex vasoconstriction that normally defends pressure on standing. Beta-1 blockade slows the heart rather than causing this orthostatic pattern, and beta-2 and muscarinic effects do not explain it.

quiz.q: A patient is lethargic with a respiratory rate of 6, pinpoint pupils, and normal skin temperature and moisture. Bowel sounds are present and there are no secretions. Which toxidrome fits, and what endpoint guides the antidote?
choices: Anticholinergic; physostigmine to normalize the pupils
Cholinergic; atropine titrated to dry secretions
Opioid; naloxone titrated to an adequate respiratory rate rather than full wakefulness
Sedative-hypnotic; flumazenil to full alertness
quiz.why: Pinpoint pupils with respiratory and mental depression and no cholinergic wetness is the opioid toxidrome, and naloxone is titrated to breathing to avoid precipitating withdrawal. Cholinergic poisoning adds SLUDGE and bradycardia, and sedative-hypnotics leave pupils relatively normal.

quiz.q: A patient who took a large dose of diphenhydramine is agitated, hyperthermic, flushed and dry, with urinary retention and absent bowel sounds. Which single physical finding most cleanly separates this from a sympathomimetic overdose?
choices: The blood pressure
The heart rate
The pupil size
The absence of sweating
quiz.why: Both toxidromes produce tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia and dilated pupils, so the skin decides: anticholinergic patients are dry and sympathomimetic patients are drenched. Vital signs and pupils overlap too much to distinguish them.

quiz.q: A trauma patient is intubated and sedated. How should the verbal component of the GCS be documented?
choices: As 1, since no words are produced
As T, indicating the verbal score cannot be assessed because of the tube
As 5, giving the benefit of the doubt
The GCS should not be recorded at all
quiz.why: An intubated patient cannot be scored verbally, so the component is recorded as T rather than guessed, and the eye and motor scores are still documented. Scoring 1 or 5 invents data, and the motor score remains the most prognostically useful part.

quiz.q: Two patients both have a GCS of 9. One is E2 V2 M5 and the other is E4 V1 M4. Why does the breakdown matter?
choices: The verbal score determines airway need
The totals are identical, so the patients are clinically equivalent
The motor component carries the most prognostic weight, so a localizing patient differs meaningfully from one who only withdraws
Eye opening is the most important component
quiz.why: The motor score is the strongest prognostic element, so M5 versus M4 describes different patients despite equal totals, which is why a bare number is nearly useless. Eye and verbal components carry less prognostic weight, and airway decisions rest on the whole picture.

quiz.q: A 7-year-old has repeated 8-second blank stares with immediate return to normal activity and no confusion afterward. Which seizure type is this?
choices: Absence
Focal with impaired awareness
Status epilepticus
Generalized tonic-clonic
quiz.why: Absence seizures are brief 5- to 15-second stares in school-age children with no postictal confusion, which is the feature that separates them from focal seizures with impaired awareness. Tonic-clonic seizures have stiffening, jerking and a prolonged postictal phase.

quiz.q: What is the underlying cellular mechanism of neuronal injury in prolonged status epilepticus?
choices: Excitotoxicity from continuous glutamate release flooding neurons with calcium
Direct mechanical damage from muscle contraction
Loss of myelin from repeated firing
Osmotic swelling from sodium loss
quiz.why: Sustained glutamate release drives calcium into neurons and kills them, while the systemic cost adds hyperthermia, lactic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis and hypoxia. Demyelination and osmotic injury are not the mechanism of seizure-related neuronal death.

quiz.q: A patient seizes for 3 minutes, stops, then seizes again 90 seconds later without regaining consciousness. How is this classified?
choices: A postictal state
Two separate provoked seizures requiring only observation
Status epilepticus, because seizures recur without full recovery of consciousness between them
Absence status
quiz.why: Status epilepticus is defined as 5 minutes or more of continuous activity OR repeated seizures without recovery of consciousness in between, and the second limb applies here. Waiting on the basis that each individual seizure was short delays treatment and lets GABA receptors internalize.

quiz.q: Which sequence correctly orders bone healing, with approximate timing?
choices: Soft callus, hematoma, hard callus, remodeling
Hematoma over hours to days, soft callus to about 3 weeks, hard callus 3 to 12 weeks, then remodeling over months
Hard callus first, then hematoma, then remodeling
Remodeling, hematoma, callus, union within 72 hours
quiz.why: Bleeding clots into a scaffold first, cartilage bridges the gap for about three weeks, woven bone unites the fracture between three and twelve weeks, and organized lamellar remodeling continues for months to years. Adult upper limb fractures unite around 6 weeks and lower limb at 12 or more.

quiz.q: A 9-month-old who cannot walk has a spiral femur fracture. Why is the pattern significant?
choices: Spiral fractures are always pathologic
Spiral fractures indicate a Salter-Harris V injury
Spiral fractures heal faster in infants
A spiral pattern requires a twisting force, which a non-ambulatory infant cannot generate, raising concern for inflicted injury
quiz.why: Spiral fractures come from torsion, and a child who cannot yet walk cannot produce that mechanism accidentally, which makes it a recognized red flag for abuse. Healing speed, pathologic bone and growth plate grading are separate issues.

quiz.q: Which pair of findings appears EARLIEST in compartment syndrome?
choices: Absent capillary refill and cool skin
Pulselessness and pallor
Pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch
Paralysis and paresthesia
quiz.why: Pressure exceeds capillary perfusion long before it occludes a major artery, so pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch come first while pulses remain present. Waiting for pallor, pulselessness or paralysis means waiting until irreversible damage, which begins within 4 to 6 hours.

quiz.q: A marathon runner collapses with a CK of 38,000 U/L, dark urine and a potassium of 6.1 mEq/L. Which two threats drive immediate management?
choices: Myoglobin-induced kidney injury and hyperkalemia, treated with aggressive IV fluid and potassium management
Hypokalemia and dehydration, treated with potassium replacement
Infection and sepsis, treated with antibiotics
Compartment syndrome only, treated with fasciotomy
quiz.why: Rhabdomyolysis releases myoglobin that injures the kidney and potassium that can be lethal, so aggressive fluid resuscitation plus treatment of hyperkalemia comes first. Potassium is high rather than low, and antibiotics do not address muscle breakdown.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old on long-term prednisone sustains a vertebral fracture after bending to lift a bag of groceries. What term describes this fracture and what mechanism explains it?
choices: Greenstick fracture from incomplete ossification
Comminuted fracture from high energy
Stress fracture from repetitive overload
Pathologic fracture through bone weakened by steroid-related osteoporosis
quiz.why: A fracture occurring with trivial force through bone weakened by tumor, infection, osteoporosis or cyst is a pathologic fracture, and chronic steroids tip the osteoblast-osteoclast balance toward resorption. Stress fractures arise from repetitive loading, and greenstick fractures occur in children.

quiz.q: Why does the periosteum matter clinically in fracture care?
choices: It is the site of red marrow production
It carries the bone's blood supply and nerves, so fractures hurt and stripped periosteum heals poorly
It is the calcium reservoir of the body
It forms the growth plate in children
quiz.why: Periosteal blood vessels and nerves explain fracture pain and the poor healing seen when it is stripped by high-energy injury or surgery. Marrow lives in cancellous bone, the calcium bank is the mineral of bone itself, and the physis is separate cartilage.

quiz.q: A 26-year-old dislocated his shoulder anteriorly. Which structure must be specifically assessed before and after reduction?
choices: The ulnar nerve at the elbow
The axillary nerve, tested over the lateral deltoid
The median nerve at the wrist
The peroneal nerve at the fibular neck
quiz.why: The axillary nerve wraps the surgical neck of the humerus and is at risk in anterior dislocation, so deltoid sensation and function are documented before and after reduction. The median nerve is the concern in a distal radius fracture and the ulnar nerve in elbow injury.

quiz.q: A patient has low back pain radiating past the knee, weak big toe extension and weak ankle dorsiflexion, with a normal Achilles reflex. Which root is involved?
choices: S1
S2
L4
L5
quiz.why: L5 supplies big toe extension and ankle dorsiflexion and has no deep tendon reflex, so the Achilles remains normal. S1 involvement would weaken plantar flexion and blunt the Achilles reflex, and L4 governs knee extension and the patellar reflex.

quiz.q: Which set of back pain features is a red flag requiring imaging rather than conservative management?
choices: Fever, unexplained weight loss, IV drug use, or night pain unrelieved by rest
Pain that improves with walking
Bilateral paraspinal muscle tenderness after moving furniture
Pain worse with prolonged sitting in a 30-year-old
quiz.why: Fever, weight loss, IV drug use, cancer history, immunosuppression, progressive deficit and night pain unrelieved by rest point toward infection, malignancy or another serious cause. Mechanical features in a young patient without red flags are managed conservatively.

quiz.q: A patient's knee locks intermittently, has joint line tenderness, and swelled gradually over a full day after a twisting injury. Which structure is most likely injured?
choices: Medial collateral ligament
Anterior cruciate ligament
Meniscus
Patellar tendon
quiz.why: Mechanical locking with joint line tenderness and a slow effusion is the meniscal pattern, since the meniscus is relatively avascular and bleeds little. An ACL tear produces a pop with a tense hemarthrosis within hours, and MCL injury gives valgus laxity.

quiz.q: In the musculoskeletal exam sequence, when are provocative special tests performed, and why?
choices: Only when x-rays are normal
Immediately after inspection
First, to localize the problem before touching the patient
Last, after inspection, palpation, range of motion, strength and neurovascular assessment, because they are provocative
quiz.why: Special tests are deliberately provocative, so they come last, after inspection, palpation, active then passive range of motion, strength grading and a documented neurovascular check. Doing them first causes pain and guarding that corrupt the rest of the exam.

quiz.q: Why is documentation of distal pulses, sensation and motor function required both before and after splinting?
choices: Because splints commonly cause nerve injury and this proves it happened
Because without a pre-splint baseline you cannot show that a deficit found afterward was not caused by the splint
Because insurance requires it
Because pulses change with every splint
quiz.why: The pre-splint check establishes the baseline, without which any post-splint deficit is indistinguishable from an iatrogenic one. The purpose is documentation of a baseline rather than an assumption that splints routinely cause injury.

quiz.q: A toddler is brought in holding her arm flexed and pronated after being lifted by the hand. There is no swelling or bruising. What is the likely diagnosis?
choices: Elbow dislocation
Supracondylar humerus fracture
Nursemaid's elbow, a radial head subluxation
Clavicle fracture
quiz.why: Traction on an extended pronated arm subluxes the radial head, producing a child who simply will not use the arm, with no swelling or deformity. Fractures and dislocations produce swelling, deformity or point tenderness.

quiz.q: Why does cartilage essentially fail to repair after injury, while bone heals reliably?
choices: Cartilage has no blood supply, so it receives none of the cells and factors that drive repair
Cartilage has too much blood supply and bleeds excessively
Cartilage regenerates but only in children
Cartilage is repaired by osteoclasts, which are slow
quiz.why: Avascular tissue cannot recruit inflammatory and progenitor cells, so cartilage does not heal in the way well-perfused bone does; ligaments and tendons are intermediate, with poor supply and slow healing. Osteoclasts resorb bone rather than repairing cartilage.

quiz.q: A patient with a large left hemispheric stroke has eyes deviated to the left. What does this gaze preference indicate?
choices: The eyes deviate toward the side of the lesion in a hemispheric stroke
Gaze deviation indicates a cerebellar lesion
Gaze deviation is always a seizure phenomenon
The eyes deviate away from the lesion
quiz.why: In a destructive hemispheric lesion the unopposed contralateral gaze centre drives the eyes toward the damaged side, away from the weak limbs. Seizures can drive gaze the other way, but a persistent preference with a fixed deficit fits a stroke.

quiz.q: Which statement about cerebrospinal fluid is correct?
choices: CSF is produced by the arachnoid granulations and absorbed by the choroid plexus
CSF does not circulate through the ventricles
About 150 mL is present at once while roughly 500 mL is produced daily, so the volume turns over about three times a day
About 500 mL is present at once and produced daily
quiz.why: The choroid plexus makes about 500 mL daily against a standing volume of roughly 150 mL, giving roughly three turnovers a day. Production is at the choroid plexus and absorption at the arachnoid granulations, in that direction, and the fluid circulates through the ventricular system.

quiz.q: Why is levodopa given for Parkinson's disease instead of dopamine itself?
choices: Dopamine is inactivated by stomach acid
Dopamine does not cross the blood-brain barrier, while levodopa does
Levodopa is a stronger receptor agonist than dopamine
Dopamine has no effect on the basal ganglia
quiz.why: Tight junctions between capillary endothelial cells exclude dopamine, so its precursor levodopa is used and converted centrally. Levodopa is not itself a receptor agonist, and dopamine acts perfectly well on basal ganglia receptors once it gets there.

quiz.q: A patient after a subarachnoid hemorrhage develops enlarging ventricles and worsening consciousness two weeks later with no new bleeding. What is the mechanism?
choices: Reduced CSF production by the choroid plexus
Cerebral atrophy causing the ventricles to appear larger
Obstructive hydrocephalus from a blocked cerebral aqueduct only
Communicating hydrocephalus from blood clogging the arachnoid granulations and preventing reabsorption
quiz.why: Subarachnoid blood impairs reabsorption at the arachnoid granulations, producing a communicating hydrocephalus in which flow is not physically obstructed. Reduced production would shrink rather than enlarge ventricles, and atrophy does not cause a declining level of consciousness over two weeks.

quiz.q: Which combination of transmitter changes best explains a seizure at the synaptic level?
choices: Excess dopamine in the basal ganglia
Excess GABA inhibition overwhelming glutamate
Glutamate excitation overwhelming GABA inhibition
Loss of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction
quiz.why: Glutamate is the brain's accelerator and GABA its brake, so a seizure represents excitation outrunning inhibition, which is why benzodiazepines that enhance GABA terminate it. Acetylcholine loss causes weakness rather than seizures, and dopamine excess produces movement and psychiatric effects.

quiz.q: A man cannot shrug his left shoulder or turn his head to the right against resistance after a neck dissection. Which cranial nerve was injured?
choices: CN XI
CN XII
CN VII
CN X
quiz.why: The spinal accessory nerve supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, so injury during neck surgery produces shoulder droop and weak head turning away from the injured side. CN VII moves the face, CN X the palate and cords, and CN XII the tongue.

quiz.q: A patient with a brainstem stroke has right-sided facial weakness with left-sided arm and leg weakness. What does this crossed pattern localize?
choices: A cervical cord lesion
A cerebellar lesion
A cortical lesion in the left hemisphere
A brainstem lesion, where a cranial nerve nucleus is affected ipsilaterally and the descending motor tract before it crosses
quiz.why: Crossed findings, cranial nerve loss on one side with limb weakness on the other, are the signature of a brainstem lesion, because cranial nerve nuclei act ipsilaterally while the corticospinal tract has not yet crossed in the medulla. A single cortical lesion would produce face and limb weakness on the same side.
